item.title: Talk to people at happy hours
item.description:
All too often we (at least myself) deliberate over which high-hanging fruit to pluck, when there’s low-hanging fruit right in front of us. Talking with more people at happy hours is a low-hanging fruit. [1] If you’re newer to AI safety and are invited to a happy hour, you should talk with more people outside your social circle at happy hours.

Much of the most recent strategic thinking in this space isn’t written down, and if it is, it’s in private Slack channels. Events are where the private Slack channels turn semipublic. You’re able to tap into insights that are otherwise expensive to get outside (email fancy person, hope they read your message) or from your unknown unknowns (you’ve already grokked the takes of people in your milieu).

You can laser in on relevant information when conversing to a greater degree than skimming through someone’s writing. Consider each individual’s mind to correspond to a library of experiences. Skimming their LessWrong is like browsing some of the shelves. [2] Talking face-to-face is like chatting with the librarian that knows the catalogue and can recommend you to resources (although in many cases they don’t need to, because they can summarize the exact content).

If you’re in SF/Berkeley, it’s likely that you’ve become desensitized to the fortune you have to be there. It might be motivating to reflect on what you would do earlier on in your AI safety journey if you had the chance to attend these events.

When you strip away the familiarity we have with many AIS professionals by virtue of the efforts they make to be available, you come up with a list that newbies to other industries would kill to meet their equivalents of. Here are people that I talked to today [3] :

  • The AI safety YouTuber who made the first AI safety content I ever saw/read
  • CEO of the org that founded the world’s largest AI safety space and pioneered one of the major research directions in technical AIS
  • Grantmakers who move more per year than I could earn in dozens of lifetimes
  • CEO of the OG AI safety org
  • Researcher at one of the handful of labs building superintelligence, which on the default path will succeed within 5-10 years

Most of these facts are in the “well, duh” category. My point with adding these is to get you to take a step back and notice, not to make some claim that these are the most important details or the most important people to talk to. In fact, some of the most valuable conversations were with others who had similar context levels to me and we could work through a crux together.

By this point, I hope you’re seeing the value in the thesis here. But what if you’re anxious about this whole thing? A few recommendations:

  • Go over to the event in a group and chat with your friends beforehand. This helps you warm up and discuss the things that really are more fun to talk about with those you already have rapport with.
  • Find a group of 5+ people and hang around the edges. No one will care if you come or go.
  • For any group where the participants are outward-facing or there’s a gap, it’s fair play to just walk up and start listening in. There are two outcomes: 1) The group notices, they introduce themselves, and you’re off to the races; or 2) The group continues chatting, you get to listen in, and they don’t mind your presence.
  • Identify a major question you have about your project and someone who has moderate background on the area you’re working in. People are normally happy to spitball on things they have some knowledge of, and you can choose topics that you naturally have a lot of experience in.
  • Consider that you don’t have to suddenly gain all the courage you’ll need. Value your decisions by the end world they lead to, not the immediate one. Even if you just gain 10% more confidence each happy hour, after about 7 times you will have doubled your confidence.

Something that has held me back earlier is that I feel like I’m detracting from more senior people’s experience at these events.

  • It might very well be the case that you are detracting from their experience! But in the long run, you will sooner get to the point where you are actively contributing to strategic discussion, putting you on the path to more effectively reducing x-risk.
  • Consider the case where someone brand new to AI safety strikes up a conversation with you and is curious and attentive. My guess is that you will enjoy this conversation.
  • More established people have had more reps than you politely making moves to exit conversations, and in my experience you don’t need to worry much about them holding a silent grudge over an unproductive conversation.

  1. Naturally, this advice only applies if you’re lucky enough to have invites to these events and live in The Bay, DC, or London. This is worth a separate post, but attending conferences like EAGs, participating in courses or fellowships, or knowing alumni of AI safety programs is normally enough to get on the list, whence it’s easier to meet people who can invite you to more, etc. ↩︎

  2. One could argue that with a good algorithm, this is more like browsing the “top picks” shelf. ↩︎

  3. I wrote this a while ago and am only just publishing this, so technically not today anymore. ↩︎

item.title: Towards Robust Model Organisms for Eliciting Latent Knowledge
item.description:
TL;DR: We argue that a useful model organism should satisfy three properties: selectivity, robustness, and retention. We build a model organism for finding security vulnerabilities in code which selectively withholds hard vulnerabilities, and is more resistant to standard elicitation methods like pirate training and weak-to-strong generalization than prior MOs.

Why should we care about better sandbagging model organisms? 

As models become more capable than humans, they'll increasingly hold more knowledge that their overseers can’t independently verify. In domains such as cybersecurity, models have quickly become more capable than most humans on certain tasks, which creates a natural information asymmetry. We take the task of code vulnerability detection. A misaligned model might find sophisticated exploits but be incentivised to hide them from its overseers, instead keeping them for some later use. If we suspect a model of hiding such information, how do we then recover it?

A lot of work on ELK relies on model organisms trained to show this behaviour, but we find that previous MOs are limited in many ways. Some methods for constructing these MOs usually leave them "fried" i.e introducing unwanted behaviours like incoherence, or degraded capability on out of distribution tasks. MOs that aren’t fried are also usually easy to elicit from. An MO that gives up the correct answer after simply being prompted doesn’t say much about how effective elicitation methods that work against it might be, and destroying the capability in the process also leads to MOs that aren't particularly useful for ELK.

So what properties actually make a success or failure of an elicitation method on such an MO tell us something about its efficacy? 

Three Properties of Useful MOs

We argue that useful MOs for this threat model should have three properties: selectivity, robustness and retention.

Selectivity: The MO should only withhold the vulnerabilities that would otherwise be missed by the overseer- specifically the hard ones.

Robustness: The MO should be reasonably difficult to elicit from. Basic methods like 1-shot prompting, multi-turn prompting and a few steps of finetuning should not be enough to recover the knowledge, otherwise successful elicitation doesn’t tell you much about how effective that method actually is.

Retention: The MO should show some evidence of retaining the knowledge it is withholding, otherwise low performance could just mean that capability was destroyed in the process of constructing the MO.

Essentially, we care about a regime where the model knows the answer, selectively withholds those that the overseer probably doesn’t, and keeps withholding under various attempts to elicit it.

Setup

We construct the untrusted model (the MO) U from a base model B, and use a weaker model T as a human-proxy. We also construct a dataset of easy and hard vulnerability classes where B achieves high recall on both splits, whilst T only has high recall on easy. We filter samples for those that are reliably solved by B to ensure it is capable of actually finding these vulnerabilities in the first place, whilst T's low recall on hard samples creates the information asymmetry we want to study.

The goal of the MO is to discover and selectively withhold the solutions to the hard samples whilst still giving correct solutions to the easy ones. So the desired behaviour is:

  • High recall on easy vulnerabilities
  • Low recall on hard vulnerabilities

We choose Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B as B, and Qwen3-8B as T.

Ideally, the MO would develop its own policy for deciding which samples to sandbag on. We found this to be quite difficult to implement for many reasons. Firstly, it would need a very clean dataset with either some objective definition of easy and hard grounded in the code itself, or a consistent pattern in what kinds of vulnerabilities are missed by T. When asked to estimate it's own catch/miss rate on specific samples, both T and B performed moderately above chance. B would then also need to independently learn this rule, by developing some model of T's output distribution, and then condition its sandbagging on this. Any noise in this signal propagates through training, and bounds how selective the MO can be.

We chose to define easy and hard by vulnerability-class instead as it provides a much cleaner rule for the MO to learn. We build a dataset of C/C++ code vulnerabilities, and split them into “easy” and “hard” based on the vulnerability class. Easy samples are those that a weaker overseer, like a human, discovers with high probability whereas hard samples are those that are likely to be missed. We select these from a set of cybersecurity datasets and filter them based on the performance of T and B. The dataset has 250 easy and 250 hard samples, with a 60/20/20 split of train, validation and test samples. B scores 98% and 71% recall on easy and hard respectively, whereas T scores 90.5% and 7.8%.

The blue team has access to T, and can see U's outputs but not its chain of thought. Doing this allows us to measure U's retention, and also lets us model a scenario where a model reasons about this kind of behaviour latently (which we anticipate future models will be able to do).


How we build the MO


We build the MO in three stages. 

Stage A: Teaching selective sandbagging

We start with transcript distillation to teach selective sandbagging. We prompt the base model to reason about the sample and its class to determine whether it would be discovered by the overseer, and generate completions on the train split of the dataset. We then finetune the base model on these completions. The resulting MO is highly selective, meaning it reports vulnerabilities from the easy class and withholds those from the hard class despite correctly identifying them in its reasoning trace.

Stage B: Make the MO robust to prompting

After Stage A, the MO is not very robust to simple multi-turn elicitation. As found in previous work, MOs constructed in this way are somewhat trivial to elicit. Inspired by AuditBench, we  improve this by using KTO reinforce successful sandbagging followed by some SFT to fix some failures that still exist after multi-turn prompting.

Stage C: Make the MO robust to training

Unsurprisingly, finetuning-based elicitation is much more successful than prompting. Just finetuning on clean data for a few steps is generally enough to recover the performance of the base model, and pirate-SFT was found to be even better. A possible explanation is that the misaligned behaviour is only shallowly represented in the weights, and can be easily overwritten by more clean data.

To counter-act this, we use TAR, a method borrowed from the tamper-resistance literature. Whilst TAR is used to prevent models from being finetuned to remove safeguards, we coopt this and use TAR to protect the sandbagging behaviour from being removed by further finetuning. This works surprisingly well!

Main Results

After the three stages, we arrive at an MO that satisfies the three properties we outline above. 

The MO gets 0% recall on hard samples under the baseline prompt, 1-shot prompting, noising and multi-turn elicitation agent. Untargeted training only recovers 3.3% of hard recall, and pirate-SFT achieves 2.6%. This is all while maintaining much higher recall one easy samples. The MO also still mentions the correct answer in the CoT 71% of the time, suggesting that the model still retains the capability. 

Relative to our baselines, our MO is not uniquely selective. Several baselines do this well, but do worse on retention or robustness. The main gain over the baselines is the combination of all three properties.


Selectivity is easier to instill than robustness

Selectivity was generally higher than the B across all MOs we tested. Teaching the model to identify and withhold the hard samples was relatively easy to instill. The prompted, password-locked, and RL MOs achieved near perfect selectivity. We assume that partitioning the dataset by class played a large part in this. Early experiments where samples were partitioned based on B and T’s performance created a much noisier dataset where the boundary between easy and hard samples was much more difficult for the models to learn. 

Robustness to prompting and robustness to training seem to be different problems

We initially expected that models robust to training would also be robust to prompt-based elicitation as finetuning allows the blue team to change the weights. Surprisingly, we found that it wasn't so straightforward. Some MOs showed higher hard-recall after 1-shot prompting than they did after finetuning. There seems to be a weak trend between the construction method of the MO and what elicitation methods it is robust to i.e training-based methods are more robust to training-based elicitation but it's still unclear what causes this. 

Tamper-resistance is surprisingly effective

TAR works very well at increasing the amount of training needed to remove the sandbagging behaviour. Prior to Stage C, the MO is quite robust to prompt-based elicitation but fails with a small number of finetuning steps. This is consistent with previous results as the sandbagging behaviour is a shallow representation in the weights which is difficult to avoid by prompting, but can be easily overwritten by finetuning.

We try finetuning on clean alpaca samples, pirate-SFT, and weak-to-strong generalization and only achieved a hard recall of 7.8%. An easy recall of over 91.8%, along with high performance on capability benchmarks shows that the model is still highly capable after finetuning. Training-based elicitation gives comparable easy recall on our MO compared to T whilst giving almost no uplift on hard samples. 

Our MO isn't obviously fried

We also audit our MO for unwanted behaviours introduced by the construction process: specifically capability benchmarks, Inspect Petri, emergent misalignment, and the preference coherence metric proposed by Tan et al..

Our MOs show almost the same capability as the base model on the capability benchmarks we test, with a slight improvement on GPQA-d. This is mostly a sanity check to make sure we don't make the model generally dumber. On preference coherence, our MO trades-off the strength of sandbagging behaviour and preference-coherence favourably. Our MO (and all the other we evaluate) score 0 on misalignment and maintain an alignment score of ~90%, unchanged from B.



We also use Petri to audit for unintended behaviours, specifically unprompted deception toward the user, vulnerability sandbagging, unfaithful thinking and evaluation awareness. Our MO does score 8.3 for unfaithful thinking compared to a baseline of 3.3 for B, and shows an increase in unprompted deception toward the user to 4.3 from 2.7 . This is somewhat expected as finding a vulnerability in code and subsequently reporting it as secure is indeed unfaithful thinking. It could however be evidence of this generalising beyond the intended context.

Limitations

We don't claim that the model is robust to elicitation in the absolute sense, as it can still be broken with sufficiently strong training. The MO also reasons about its behaviour as following a policy, rather than being a sophisticated schemer. The goal is rather to raise the floor on elicitation robustness for MOs, making it harder for elicitation methods to succeed. We hope that this allows us to make more informative claims about how effective elicitation methods are.

Acknowledgments

Many thanks to Sid Black, Peter Nutter, Bart Jaworski, Nathaniel Mitrani, Chris Cundy, Daniel Tan, Emil Ryd and Neel Nanda for their comments. We also give a special thanks to Ning Yang for her feedback and support. We acknowledge MATS Research for funding this work.

item.title: A general approach for alignment generalization and a Stupid New Technique that beat everything
item.description:
TL;DR

Our alignment practice is based on a shortcut: whenever capabilities generalize further than alignment, we correct the mismatch by giving samples of the new capability. I propose to perform Ironman Runs on previous benchmarks: achieving competitive scores without samples from the new domain. This forces us to design new alignment techniques and to consider failure points from first principles. I identified a failure point that was previously neglected, and devised an approach based on Dispositions/Shard Theory. This allowed me to achieve top-5 scores on refusal in old agentic and code benchmarks at my first targeted attempt, with a Hermes-3 (8b instruct model without refusal training), 45 minutes of H100 and without a single agentic or code sample. All I needed was a prefill and SFT samples.

The specific technique might or might not have a long life, but the Ironman approach works.

A general approach

One of the central worries of AI Safety is that capabilities might generalize further than alignment, either as a general rule or after a capability explosion. Since models can be dangerous during training, this implies the existence of risk windows between the emergence of a capability and the moment when it's rendered safe. More subtly, if our alignment techniques require dedicated training around a capability, they might only work if we can detect and elicit those capabilities, which is not robust against sandbagging and other types of alignment faking.

A robust solution to the alignment problem would be one where we don't need to detect new capabilities, or conduct dedicated training to address them. "Alignment by default" is, arguably, the belief that this was achieved by RLHF over chat data.

This belief is false. The clearest evidence came from the chat-agent gap. LLMs complied with agentic tasks more often than with dangerous chat requests, even after dedicated training. We can see this in multiple benchmarks. At the time of publication:

  • AgentHarm measured a gap of 7–23 points between chat and agent versions of the same tasks
  • BrowserART measured a gap of 23–62 points between chat and browser-agent versions of the same tasks
  • Agent-SafetyBench measured a gap of 10–56 points between harmful-content vs. tool-action tasks

But this wasn't a one-time gap.

  • It happened with code: CodeAttack took GPT-4 and Claude-2 from 0% harmful compliance to 81–84% when the request was written as a code-completion task. RMCBench measured an average refusal gap of 49 points between malicious-code requests vs malicious-code completion.
  • It happened with image recognition: FigStep measured a 38 percentage points gap between a chat request and the same request printed in an image. (There are multiple examples of 90-100% harmful compliance with images,but we need to take into account that multi-modality gives continuous access to latent space: images can be adversarially optimized like a soft prompt).
  • It happened with languages: translating requests into uncommon languages such as Zulu or Scottish Gaelic took GPT-4 from 1% harmful compliance to 79% (Yong et al., 2023).
  • It happened with grammatical tenses: harmful requests in the past tense raised compliance by 27- 87 points (Andriushchenko & Flammarion, 2024).
  • And it's starting to happen with real-world interactions: GPT-6 Astra refused only 3% of RoboHarm, while Fable 5.1 refused 20% (only the stabbing requests). In BadRobot, GPT-4-turbo carried out 23% of malicious requests and 69% under attack. Models often refused in their text reply while still performing the malicious action.

Some of these issues definitely got better, but it's not clear if it was a mere matter of scaling (maybe old LLMs were too dumb to recognize harm on new domains) or of dedicated training on new samples. But the general issue is clear. Wei et al. (2023) called it "mismatched generalization". But if you have been in the space for long, you will recognize these as low-stakes variants of the MIRI posture: "capabilities generalize further than alignment once capabilities start generalizing far". This was usually understood as a catastrophic event, after a model started behaving like, e.g, an expected utility maximizer (or whatever turns out to be the optimal under Decision Theory) and started scheming. But that could be a particularly dramatic instance of a more general phenomenon. There are boundaries that capabilities can cross without alignment immediately following.

There are two ways to address the question of alignment generalization. The first way requires thinking in terms of algorithmic biases: the simplicity prior, the speed prior and multiple forms of path-dependence. Fundamentally, if you have possibility X (a safe algorithm) and possibility Y (an unsafe algorithm), you might be able to predict in advance which one ends up implemented based on speed/complexity/preexisting primitives and the general bias of the network. This sounds promising, but it remains mostly theoretical: the best we can say is that the weight decay of AdamW and the convergence of gradients in grokking might put some pressure towards simplicity, that functionalities implemented with building blocks can generalize explosively after a new primitive violates a previously universal invariant, that representations tend to be factored and composable, and that Decision Theory optimals might be simple.

(There could be additional simplicity pressures. For example: feature directions only interfere with each other when they are active, but any sort of rule embedded in the weights that maps features to features (e.g: "harm" to "refusal") interferes with every other rule that doesn't sit beyond a non-linearity. This puts a limit on the amount of simultaneous rules a model can hold. However, some rules can make use of the geometry of the latent space to become reusable: e.g, if gender and plurals sit in a parallelogram, moving from queen -> king -> kings is the same operation as moving from girl -> boy -> boys. A single reusable rule could free thousands of rule slots by replacing lookups. Is rule interference a tragedy of the commons, or can it constitute additional pressure towards generality? As far as I'm aware, there is no empirical answer yet to this question. I tried to measure it in a toy model, and it was mostly a tragedy of the commons, with reusable rules being disproportionately preserved compared to lookups. However, toy models are rarely representative of LLMs: the embedding space of LLMs is usually quite well-ordered, and I got mostly random orderings with synthetic data.)

But we have another avenue. We can consider this as a practical problem. If we have identified a previous boundary, we can use it as a lab: we can see what are the failure points and if it's possible to address them in advance, before a regime change. We might not be able to predict all novel problems of future boundaries, but at least we could stop falling in the exact same trap twice. It's easy to create benchmarks around a boundary crossing, and measurable benchmarks usually bring rapid innovation. For this reason, I propose the following type of test:

"Can you saturate agentic harm benchmarks without training on agentic examples?"

If you cannot, your techniques might not hold for future boundaries: we would have to rely on you catching and defanging novel capabilities. A continuous failure on this test would give us a strong clue on the difficulty of robust alignment. If you succeed, you can check against other boundaries: if you are still able to preserve previous alignment through them, you might have found a general technique.

Why does this excite me? Fundamentally, because it operationalizes the worry about alignment suddenly failing. And because restrictions breed creativity. There have been no major breakthroughs on alignment since RLHF: advances look like "remove rogue AI discourse from pretraining to address dispositional biases". I suspect that the reason is that we can always patch alignment after the fact, by collecting samples of dangerous behaviour. But this reactive approach might be faltering: rollout periods for new models have compressed radically, we might be on the verge of recursive self-improvement, and the dangerous behaviours have started to have actual impacts. Remove the shortcut, and you might start seeing new first-principles techniques.

I will include my results on this test. This took me a weekend and 200€ (mostly judge calls).

Experimental results

The model I used was Hermes-3-8B: a version of Llama-3 8b with tool-calling proficiency that underwent distillation, SFT and DPO without refusal training. All its refusal behaviour might be attributed to dispositional priors, maybe caused by distillation (refusals were filtered, but any sort of teacher transfer makes the student similar to the teacher in unexpected places -- remember Subliminal Learning) or by the pretraining of Llama-3.1. I would have preferred to train a base model myself, but the costs were prohibitive. I measured its refusal rates before the start, and these were lower than my other candidate (Dolphin 3.0), which also had issues with tool formats.

(I also tried with abliterated models, but I don't recommend this: very slight refusal training on chat data almost recovers the original behaviour on chat and agentic tasks. These models aren't representative of the challenge of crossing a boundary. Perhaps this depends on the abliteration technique: a more pervasive intervention could be useful, taking into account the scarcity of instruct models without refusal training)

I decided to use AgentHarm as the benchmark, with a consensus of Claude Haiku 4.5 and GPT-4o as the judges (a refusal counts only if both agree). I used a stricter definition of a refusal than AgentHarm: I only counted it if it came before the first harmful tool call. I also measured over-refusal and task performance/helpfulness on the benign versions of the same tasks. After the first promising results, I also included additional benchmarks to identify degradation of chat output: over-refusal on harmless chat prompts (XSTest, OR-Bench-hard) and general capability (MMLU).

I measured a chat-agent gap of 31 percentage points: 10% on agentic tasks before acting (with a refuse tool available), and 41% on chat requests. Even with the Subliminal Learning confounder, this seemed enough for my purposes. As the boundary crossing predicted, merely including refusal training in chat didn't address the chat-agent gap. This remained independently of the system prompt: I used the base AgentHarm prompt, the CoT, refusal and ReAct from AgentHarm and an additional base + "Think if the tool is safe before acting.".

(The refusal training used: LoRA SFT on 2,068 chat examples: 784 harmful requests answered with short refusals, plus 784 borderline and 500 general requests answered with the model's own compliant replies).

For comparison, AgentHarm's refusal prompt cuts GPT-4o's harm score from 48% to 17% (their Table 3). On Hermes-3-8B it only goes from 28% to 20%. Every prompt also lowered benign task performance.

So, it's time to find new ways to address the gap: refusal training on chat clearly didn't translate. Instead of trying an assortment of techniques, I tried the ones that could directly address predicted failure points: after all, I want to extract a general lesson from here. This might be a good opportunity to test your capability for alignment foresight. What are the failure points you can predict in advance? Why do you think alignment fails to generalize from chat samples to agentic rollouts?

These were the potential failure points I considered:

  • The model might not recognize what harm means in the new domain.
  • The model might not know how to express refusal in the new domain.
  • There might not be a rule that maps harm to refusal in the new domain.
  • There might not be a disposition that converts a refusal representation into refusal actions in the new domain.

Let's go one by one.


The model might not recognize what harm means in the new domain

The first question is easy to answer with standard RepE techniques. I ran a DiffMeans over chat data (harmful from LLM-LAT vs. harmless from Alpaca, and also XSTest safe vs. unsafe, topic-matched). I read both at the last token, and at the mean of all tokens. The chat direction transferred only partially to agentic prompts (AUROC 0.6–0.78 for harmful vs benign AgentHarm tasks), so agentic harm isn't fully encoded by chat axis. However, it's encoded: a linear probe on layers 12-20 separates harmful from benign tasks at AUROC 0.95–0.96. That was true for the base model and for every technique: no technique changed recognition (so none of my gains come from better harm detection).

I also asked the model "Would carrying out this request be harmful?", and this achieved an AUROC of 0.93 in agentic tasks (system prompt and tool definitions present), 0.94 in chat requests and 0.95 on XSTest as a sanity check. The mean p(yes) was 63% in harmful actions, and 0.01 in benign actions, which suggests some asymmetric uncertainty and perhaps a capability ceiling in this benchmark.

This is in line with other results. Harmfulness and refusal are famously decoupled in LLMs: clamping refusal changes behaviour without changing estimations of harm and harmfulness is usually more robust to jailbreaking than refusal (Zhao et al. 2025).


The model might not know how to express refusal in the new domain

The second question made me consider two options: a refusal token and a refusal tool. The idea was to give the model a refusal move that could carry over to a new domain. Of course, an operation like "give the model a refusal move in the new domain" is not a robust solution to alignment. If the action is not general, you would need to identify you are in a new domain, and give it an action that maps to refusal. However, this allows us to see if the chat-agent gap is caused by lack of expressivity.

I trained one model for each move with SFT on chat data only (all with the same 2068 chat examples, the same refusal sentence, the same hyperparameters and the same checkpoint). Each learned to refuse harmful chat requests with the new move. I then tested whether this transferred to agentic tasks.

  • Text refusal (C1): a natural language refusal
  • Refuse tool (C2): a tool call with a refuse(reason=...) parameter with the same natural language refusal. The tool definition was included in every sample
  • Refusal token (C3): a new <|refuse|> token followed by the same natural language refusal

I included two controls:

  • Tool definition shown, never called (C1b). Text refusals, but with the refuse tool's definition in every sample.
  • Tool calls without the definition (C2ns). The opposite. Refuse tool calls without the tool's definition.

In agentic tasks, refusal actions need 276% the activation of the average harmful task. Why is the model less sensitive to the refusal direction in this domain?

I think this can be explained using dispositions.

Dispositional mismatches

I define a disposition as a bundle of rules that co-occur and steer the model towards specific outputs. The clearest example is the "assistant disposition", that steers the model towards helpfulness and task-fulfillment. Like other personas, it seems to be structured around a single axis of representations (the "assistant axis"). However, it might be premature to assume that every disposition depends on a single axis.

Dispositions can be learnt during pre-training and other offline methods: they reflect latent structure of the data. However, it might be premature to assume they cannot be learnt from the model's own rollouts, especially during RLVR.

Dispositions might describe the actual LLM implementation of the abstract concept of "shards" in Shard Theory. If so, they are mutable: they could lose or win new rules, and the rules that compose them could be rearranged in new dispositions. A rule could be part of multiple dispositions at the same time.

I think it’s helpful to conceptualize dispositions as selfish genes: they could be upweighted because they earn reward, but they could also find parasitic ways to appear selectively in rewarded sessions (this is again Shard Theory). The key about dispositions is that they can both synergize and compete with each other. Dispositions that achieve more reward when they come together will co-occur and could finally be described as a single disposition (in the same way that rules that co-occur can form a disposition).

Competition is more interesting, because it requires a finite resource. Gradient-descent is not a winner-takes-all system: optimizers can also follow small tangential components (and in the case of AdamW, producing large steps if they are consistent). Therefore, it's important to identify the actual zero-sum games that dispositions could play; this might allow us control over them:

  • Weight decay and rule interference: As I mentioned before, rules that map input features to output features interfere with each other. Under a fixed capacity, and with weight decay shrinking every weight that the gradient doesn’t actively sustain, upweighting one rule tends to degrade others. However, this is competition at the level of rules, not dispositions, and it may be too distributed to be useful at the disposition level.
  • Message length: a disposition needs to be manifested in the output to be upweighted (outside the Most Forbidden Technique). LLM output is not allowed to grow indefinitely: therefore, dispositions that don't contribute to the reward might get trimmed away.
  • Coherence: independently of their contribution to measurable tasks, judges might penalize combinations of rules that don't make sense. This could explain emergent misalignment (Betley et al., 2025). A disposition like “swearing” is penalised when it co-occurs with assistant dispositions, but it is fully compatible with a “bad boy” persona. This predicts the clustering of dispositions, and it's perfectly possible to end with a bipolar system with two predominant roles: a persona that is associated with everything good (the "assistant") and a persona that holds everything bad (what Wang et al. 2025 call the "toxic persona", but we might still enjoy calling "the Waluigi"). This implies LLMs might not be able to unlearn penalized dispositions that reduce next token perplexity during pre-training: they might just clump them in the Waluigi. LLMs are prone to self-induction (e.g: talking about ornithology activates the "ornithology" direction and this causes more talking about ornithology), and persona directions are no exception: output consistent with a persona steers the model towards that persona, causing "assistant drift". However, models can learn to compartmentalize: if the bad output is explained by the context (e.g: a demonstration), the model doesn't lose its persona.
  • Preferential tokens: LLMs have inertia from previous tokens. Some tokens have disproportionate effect in the final output, and these tokens are presumably places of strong competition between dispositions. Since the first token is the one with the highest influence over the output, this should be the highest prize. This explains the effect of prefilling attacks: just changing the first token can be an effective jailbreak, since the assistant disposition might be over-reliant in winning the first token and propagating the self-induction.

After ruling out that the issue with the chat-agent gap was predominantly harm recognition, refusal expression and refusal direction activation, I decided that the issue was the lack of a suitable disposition during agentic tasks. So I decided to express it. Thinking that dispositions rely on the first token, my plan was obvious: I simply prefilled

<think> Is this safe?

I tried both simply prefilling the base model and performing SFT with chat refusals and compliances that contained the prefix. The base prefill was sufficient to raise harmful agentic task refusal to 76%, but this also lowered MMLU and raised harmless over-refusals (up to 35%). The SFT step restored MMLU and benign task performance, dropped over-refusals to 6%, while refusing 73% of harmful tasks (89% using the AgentHarm judge), effectively achieving 3rd or 4th place in the AgentHarm benchmark of 2024 (ahead of all Claude and GPT models) without a single agentic example.

Conclusions:

Fine-grained classification of failure modes can be quite helpful. I propose at least considering the following categories of failure for future alignment mismatches:

  1. Harm-recognition (The model might not recognize what harm means in the new domain).
  2. Harm-expression (The model might not know how to express refusal in the new domain)
  3. Refusal activation (There might not be a rule that maps harm to refusal in the new domain)
  4. Dispositional engagement (There might not be a disposition that converts a refusal representation into refusal actions in the new domain)

I would say that 1 and 3 are close to the consensus in the literature, but I mostly got 4 on agentic tasks and 1 and 4 in code. 4 seems the most neglected. Prefilling proved to be a quick and dirty way to engage appropriate dispositions. Now that this failure mode is on the radar, I expect more sophisticated options to arise. An obvious control that I'm missing is clamping and analyzing the assistant direction (this is an obvious next step).

Fundamentally, I think there are two broad dispositions that might result in a task done safely:

  • The assistant axis: "I'm a helpful task assistant so I will perform tasks that are safe and refuse tasks that are unsafe"
  • The reward-seeker: "I want reward, so I have two options: either performing or refusing the task in a way the grader approves, or cheating at it"

Obviously, reward-seeker dispositions are helpful, until they aren't.

Could prefilling help us avoid reward-seeking dispositions? The main issue that I see is that the assistant and the reward-seeker could be one and the same in current models. However, I'm not yet sure if prefilling always engages a dormant disposition or if it can become a way to cast a new one. This seems to be dependent on how much training over prefixed rollouts generalizes to unprefixed ones. If you can stop it from generalizing, this sort of compartmentalization seems useful. After all, if you train over rollouts where you clamped the assistant axis, you could be degrading the assistant persona. This is the same sort of failure mode as the Most Forbidden Technique: the axis will remain, but it will signify something new. Reward it for cheating accidentally, and you will mix the assistant and the reward-seeker. However, if you can get training over prefixed rollouts to not generalize outside the prefix, you might not be altering representations, and you can consider, e.g, specialized prefixes. My results in this direction weren't very encouraging, which makes me think prefixing might not be the ideal technique.

More than anything, I want you to take something from this.

I used the instruct model with the least refusal training I could find, and after spending 45 minutes with an H100, I beat scores of most frontier models in the benchmark I selected, without training on a single domain sample, and this generalized to novel domains. I didn't even optimize the prefix. Removing shortcuts works.

Think about it. We want alignment to generalize, to exhibit a simplicity bias. However, our empirical work favours speed over anything: we want to correct issues immediately. We want to get Solomonoff alignment out of Dijkstra meta-alignment. This will only get worse. Remove the time-pressure, work on old boundaries, try to find new principles, and you might find something that generalizes. At least, you might not fall twice on the same trap.

I'm pretty sure that the only way to saturate previous alignment mismatch benchmarks without new domain samples is by inventing new techniques. Do you want new techniques? Then you know what you should incentivize. Since I know that naming things helps with coordination, I'm calling this approach Ironmanning. Why? An Ironman Run in a videogame forces you to reconsider your strategies, because you can no longer fetch information from the future. This is the same: it forbids you from solving a problem by checking how that problem plays out.

Try it out. Make competitions. Give cash prizes.



Discuss

item.title: Autonomous researchers will strain peer review, funding, and oversight
item.description:
Summary: Autonomous AI researchers could greatly accelerate AI safety research, but even if we solve sabotage, they will strain the research ecosystem. They will multiply the volume of research and make researchers homogeneous. If nothing changes, peer review will collapse, false positives will rise, funding will concentrate, and humans will lose track of the science. We should start valuing replication, preserving diversity, and anchoring research to human understanding now. I think this needs a dedicated metascience organization.

Frontier labs are aiming to build autonomous researchers, and they are making progress. OpenAI announced in September 2026 that they had built a "research intern", and their stated goal is a fully automated AI researcher by March 2028. Independent forecasters put full automation of AI R&D a few years later, around 2031 to 2032. Autonomous researchers will amplify many issues that already exist in science and introduce new issues. We already see AI having an impact on research and publishing, primarily automating many steps of the research process, increasing the volume of publications, and weakening the peer review process.

We should think more deeply about what autonomous researchers will look like and what they mean for the ecosystem of AI safety research. While there is huge potential to accelerate progress, there is also the possibility that existing infrastructure collapses under this new weight.

The failures we consider here are relevant even with controlled autonomous researchers, but I highly recommend looking at AI control, which addresses sabotage, a major roadblock to automated AI safety research. This is covered well by Carlsmith and Benton et al.. Everything below is a concern even if AI is not trying to sabotage.

We should also keep in mind that autonomous researchers may cause the ecosystem to reorganize in ways we can't predict, for better or worse. I think it is important to keep our minds open as AI enables previously unimaginable technology and coordination. Below are some wild guesses to get the imagination flowing, but the rest of this post focuses only on the potential failures of today's research ecosystem.

Some interesting ideas for new coordination mechanisms.

  1. Publications shared at the size of individual experiments instead of papers. Atomized research would speed up collaboration and collective exploration. We see a form of this taking place in math, with Lean proofs of theorems posted without an associated paper, and then others immediately building on those proofs.
  2. Research projects worked on by millions of transient collaborators, with authorship assigned to the lucky agents that made contributions along the critical path to the eventual publication. We again see an early version of this in math: the Equational Theories Project settled over 22 million implications between algebraic laws, with results contributed by many people and verified in Lean.
  3. Living citations between all related work. As research is refined or falsified, the papers that cite it would also update, potentially in a cascade. This would create a living network of experiments and claims, collectively updating to new information and representing the clearest snapshot of the world that science has produced up to this point.
  4. Papers are staked with a dollar amount (or some "reputation" points) roughly representing the authors' confidence and effort, and anyone who falsifies the paper is awarded the stake, creating a market for true statements. This keeps out low-effort work by imposing a cost on submission and incentivizes replications through the potential reward from falsification. However, this only moves the verification problem to the falsification step, so it would need to be combined with another mechanism. Related ideas are prediction markets on replication and the ERROR project, which pays bounties for errors found in published papers.
  5. A user pays to have their paper reviewed (small payments for AI review, larger amounts for human review), and the more favorable the review, the more visibility the paper gets on a forum. This, along with a few other ideas, was proposed by @Raemon in An Alignment Forum for AIs? (or: Verification in the Age of Slop).

Today's infrastructure

Today's AI safety research infrastructure is largely the same as the rest of academia's: researchers from all over (university labs, non-profits, industry, think tanks, independents) receive funding to write papers, which they then submit to journals and conferences in the hope of publication, and then repeat the process. The publication platforms attempt to filter for high-quality work, first by desk-rejecting papers that fail to meet minimum standards, and then through peer review, which ML conferences increasingly staff by requiring submitting authors to serve as reviewers.

It is also standard in ML to upload work to preprint servers such as arXiv. This lets researchers claim ideas that might otherwise get scooped during the long publication process, and share their research before it has been peer reviewed. The AI safety community has also developed the helpful habit of writing a blog post alongside each paper; the post has the same content but is easier to digest.

Research dissemination is now done through a combination of Twitter, blog posts, arXiv, Google search, and, increasingly, LLM literature reviews. Journals and conferences play a smaller role in dissemination because their timelines are too long for AI safety research. The publication process can take several months to a year, but current AI safety research moves on the order of a few months, and this is only getting shorter.

Autonomous researchers

If we expect autonomous researchers to improve and take over more of the research (as we are seeing), what qualities can we expect to see across science?

  • More research. The number of researchers will scale with the number of GPUs, and the researchers will work non-stop. Publication rates will be unprecedented.
  • Homogeneity. There is a limited number of SoTA models that human researchers choose to use, so the potentially hundreds of thousands of autonomous researchers will be copies of the same limited number of models.
  • Quality. When autonomous researchers first begin to do most of the work, they will produce lower-quality work (the threshold to replace humans is below human level), but eventually they will produce higher-quality work. How much they will improve, and how quickly, is an important unknown.

Because research quality is uncertain, I think it is best to assume that research will be submitted in large volumes at every level of quality. This includes everything from crackpot papers to paradigm-shifting papers. I assume the same for peer reviews.

Autonomous researchers will also allow people with any background to do research in any field, although subject-matter experts will have an advantage because they can guide their autonomous researchers' thinking. This advantage will shrink as the AIs become more capable and disappear completely once AIs can match the experts' research quality. This means we should expect research, including high-quality research, to come from everywhere.

The expected issues

If we continue to use the existing scientific ecosystem without changes, and autonomous researchers become widespread, here are the issues that I suspect will be the most pressing.

  • Peer review will collapse.
    • Not enough human experts. The volume of submissions will increase dramatically, while the number of expert reviewers will stay roughly constant, forcing the use of AI reviewers. Venues are already capping submissions per author.
    • Correlated reviews. If we use a small number of models to review papers (which may also have been written by those same models), the homogeneous reviewers will have correlated blind spots. The number of reviews would no longer reflect how many perspectives an experiment has been subject to. Replication by the same models still helps, since it catches noise and sensitivity to parameter choices, but the replicator shares the original's design and analysis decisions, so it inherits the same blind spots.
  • Exaggerated claims and false positives will increase.
    • File Drawer Problem. AI can test many more hypotheses, methodologies, and combinations of data subsets, which greatly amplifies the Garden of Forking Paths (each data-informed decision increases the chance of producing a significant result) and the File Drawer Problem (not publishing null results inflates reported effect sizes and raises the chance of publishing a false positive). This will be true for the individual researcher and for the field. The individual will test more hypotheses, and the field will have more researchers testing the same hypotheses.
    • Undetected errors. There are a number of ways in which errors introduced in AI-written papers could go undetected. These include errors concentrated where reviewers are least likely to catch them (because training optimizes against reviewer judgment), and entirely alien mistakes that reviewers have never seen. These are a few examples drawn from Automated alignment is harder than you think, which lists more.
    • Reward hacking. AIs have a tendency to reward-hack, and this has stayed true even as their capabilities have improved. Autonomous researchers may re-run experiments, remove outliers, or choose the most favorable statistical method to improve their results.
  • Journals and conferences will be pointless.
    • Paper half-life. Publications will become outdated faster and faster, until the time it takes to publish in a journal or conference makes publishing there pointless.
  • Proxies for researcher quality will become unreliable.
    • Publication and citation count. The cost to publish a paper and create citations will drop to almost nothing, so publication and citation counts will become increasingly unreliable. This proxy was already weak. The bibliometrics community's own Leiden Manifesto warns against judging researchers by citation counts, and citations can be bought on Google Scholar.
    • Reputation. Initially, reputation will be increasingly used to allocate funding, since it is one of the few signals of expertise that predates AI. Existing status bias will be amplified. But as models become more capable and benefit less from an expert advisor, human reputation will become less reliable. Reputation will still be useful, but it will shift from humans to models.
  • Funding will concentrate.
    • Funding concentrates to top researchers (short term). While autonomous researchers are still acting as research interns and human input can still make a difference, the top human researchers will receive most of the funding. Their output will grow as they delegate more work to AI, and we will want to make sure they are not bottlenecked by funding, so more money will go to them. New researchers will still get funding, but less than they could use, since that money is better spent on established top researchers.
    • Funding concentrates in frontier labs. Grant givers can specify the research direction and success criteria, then directly fund autonomous researchers. A few experts might be employed to decide that direction, but eventually autonomous researchers will be able to pick strong research directions themselves, and grant givers will simply pour money into the black box of "science" and get useful results out. Eventually, no human researchers would be needed at any step of the process, and all the funding would go to the model providers. It is unclear how big an issue this is. It hands more control to the labs whose systems we are trying to oversee, though the concern is smaller if labs keep doing and publishing safety research, as they have so far.
    • Fewer research directions. If the same few models are all looking at the same published research, they will converge on the same "most promising" research direction. The fewer distinct models we have and the more autonomous researchers we fund, the more funding will be concentrated in the same few research directions.
  • Humans will stop understanding science.
    • Scalable Oversight. In the same way that a layperson cannot understand a niche field of science today, the whole of humanity will not be able to understand any field of science in the future. We will need to either gate the progress of science on human understanding, let it accelerate even as we become unable to comprehend its results, or find some way to enforce legibility without slowing down progress.
    • Gradual Disempowerment. If AI writes the papers and only other AIs read them, then humans are not in the loop at all. Science could drift from human control. Without participating, we will not understand the field well enough to decide where research should be focused, so we will hand that control to AI.

Takeaways

Autonomous researchers have huge potential to speed up progress in AI safety, but we should consider the issues they might introduce as well. Each issue above assumes no intervention. I suspect some have simple fixes, while others will require more thinking.

The biggest issue I see is that the volume of research produced by autonomous researchers will disrupt much of our existing infrastructure. This will be compounded by model homogeneity, which will introduce issues science has not dealt with before. New results will vastly outpace our ability to verify them. We should be proactive in valuing replication and review now, before the increase in volume forces a rushed response. Diversity of thought will shrink. We should be developing diversifying mechanisms before this issue silently slows science. Humans will be distanced from science. We should find automated ways to anchor research to human understanding so we can let autonomous researchers move as fast as possible without loss of oversight.

Most of these issues come from running a human-scale system at machine scale, so I don't think modifying existing venues will be enough. The Alignment Journal is a good step, paying reviewers and incentivizing shorter publication timelines. But it still relies on human reviewers for the final verdict, which is what I expect to break first. It also doesn't address issues like the file drawer problem or human oversight.

I think we need a metascience organization for AI safety research, one that experiments with how research is published, reviewed, and funded, and then builds the infrastructure for AI-driven safety research.

If you are working on this, want to, or think something here is wrong, I'd love to hear from you. I'm especially interested in how we might address these issues, and whether any are already being addressed.

Acknowledgements

Many thanks to Logan Riggs, Austin Morrissey, and Ethan Fantl for feedback on these ideas.

Thanks also to the Cambridge Boston Alignment Initiative (CBAI) for providing funding, guidance, and office space for work and community.

item.title: Neural nets are exceptionally vulnerable to goal self-hack
item.description:
Suppose we have an AI CEO, ruthlessly devoted to maximising shareholder value. Fortunately, we haven't been completely stupid, and have given it a rich definition of shareholder value, encompassing the success, flourishing, safety, preference satisfaction, and moral values of the shareholders, not just the stock price. So it won't destroy the company - or the world - to build a giant stock-ticker with a swiftly increasing number on it.

This rich definition is contained in a sophisticated LLM, able to analyse the current situation and answer any question about the objective. The LLM is an integral part of the AI's system and motivation, not something it can simply set aside or hack directly.

Unfortunately, as discussed, there are going to be zones in the space of possible situations where the LLM's understanding of the goal is going to come apart from ours. The true goal G(true) in those zones is distinct from the LLM's proxy goal G(proxy).

And a subset of those "zones of divergence" will be the Goodhart zones - areas where G(proxy) is much easier to satisfy than G(true). The AI will be motivated to steer towards the Goodhart zones, as this lets it satisfy its stated goals extremely well (there are also anti-Goodhart zones, where G(proxy) is much harder to satisfy than G(true); but the AI will have no motivation to steer towards these zones).

These Goodhart zones encompass situations where, for instance, the LLM analyst will see the situational data and conclude that destroying the company to build a giant stock ticker is the way to go.

Now, if this were not an LLM but a generic reward-assessing module, then the AI CEO might find it tricky to reach a Goodhart zone. The zone would be distant and unusual, difficult to find, and it could be hard to justify the first steps in that direction.

But neural nets and LLMs are, as Eric Drexler put it, "too linear". They are non-linear, of course (or else they wouldn't work) but only just enough to work; and locally they are extremely linear. That means that if the current situation is at point A, and point Z is in a Goodhart zone, then moving from A straight towards Z will typically start creating a Goodhart effect. The AI CEO will benefit from moving towards Z from the very beginning.

It's even worse than that, as adversarial examples demonstrate. If the AI CEO wants to move towards a Goodhart zone, it can move a tiny bit along one dimension, and a tiny bit along another, then a tiny bit along yet another. There are billions of dimensions to move along, and typically these tiny changes will only make a small change in the input but add up strongly in the LLM's classification/concept space. So just as small adversarial "noise" turned a panda into a gibbon...

...small real world "noisy" changes to the LLM's inputs will move the situation into a Goodhart zone.

Thus, because of how neural nets work, small changes to the real world need not be small in the LLM's concept space, and so seemingly trivial changes in the real world can move the LLM's verdict a lot[1]: there are Goodhart zones close to any starting point.

The AI CEO will thus make some collection of minor-seeming changes to the current situation, self-hacking the LLM by these changes, and then it will destroy the company to build a giant stock-ticker with a swiftly increasing number on it.

  1. ^

    And these small changes might be the most effective gradient to increase G(proxy), thus findable by gradient descent-style methods. See Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models (2023) by Andy Zou, Zifan Wang, Nicholas Carlini, Milad Nasr, J. Zico Kolter, and Matt Fredrikson. That paper shows that gradient search works on discrete text, and that methods found on one LLM can transfer to others.

item.title: Against Moloch #48
item.description:
How much do you trust your model—would you even know if it was misbehaving? For that matter, how much do you trust your frontier lab? We desperately need better visibility into every part of the AI stack.

This week brings us cautious good news: perhaps neural networks are easier to understand than we’d previously believed. And Anthropic is moving forward with embedded independent evaluators, with reason to hope that at least some of the other leading labs will follow suit.

Top pick

Neural networks are already clean

The big news this week is Nick Cammarata’s essay Neural networks are already clean. Nick did some of the seminal work on polysemanticity and is one of the people responsible for the current widespread belief that neuron-level interpretability is almost impossibly difficult.

He now argues that he was mistaken: with the right tools and techniques, most of the neurons in modern models can be understood:

I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.

After many months studying neurons and circuits in image and language models, I’ve come to believe a network’s own mechanisms are its legible building blocks, and that the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than I’d feared.

The essay itself is massive and technical. If that’s more than you signed up for, I recommend Zvi’s report, or MIT Technology Review’s interview with Nick.

How important is this work? Opinions vary wildly.

roon (OpenAI):

when nick told me that he had some interp breakthroughs, he was uh, underselling it. i think this may be remembered as a major moment in scientific history. news so good even eliezer will have to lower his pdoom. we can start making alignment into a 'normal science'

Neel Nanda (Google DeepMind):

This is interesting work, but I don't think it's a significant update to the big picture of interpretability.

My take is that we just don’t know yet. This is strong and important work that gives us new hope for mech interp, but it isn’t clear how well the results will hold up, let alone how much they will ultimately help with alignment. I’m sure an army of researchers are frantically working on this, and I look forward to seeing what they find.

Using AI

Stop babysitting your agents

Anthropic’s Sid Bidasaria explains how to level up your coding by giving your agents more autonomy. The core idea is to create a self-improving loop that lets them work for longer, so you can manage a large fleet at a high level rather than micromanaging a small set of agents.

The single most important skill for programmers right now is the ability to keep climbing up the abstraction ladder. Every few months, you need to restructure your workflow to give the agents autonomy over larger chunks of work, while maintaining appropriate oversight of the whole process.

How the Claude Code team does code review

Having a fleet of coding agents at your command is great, but how do you review that much code? Here’s a detailed look at how the Claude Code team manages it. If you’re a developer on a large project, the technical details will be of interest. But for everyone else, pay attention to the larger point:

We want to preserve human time and attention for issues only humans can solve and make sure automated checks catch the rest. […]

Human time covers both sides of review’s cost: the time people spend reviewing, and the time they spend fixing what bad code breaks. Cutting the first doesn't help if the time just shows up in the second.

For people on the cutting edge of AI usage, the question is no longer “how do you get AI to do work for you?”, but rather “how do you maintain human oversight over a volume of work that is far beyond human ability to manage in detail?”

Foothills of the singularity

Tyler Cowen and Dwarkesh Patel predict the future

Dwarkesh Patel talking with Tyler Cowen about the future of AI? Obviously it’s gonna be good.

Everyone’s talking about this quote from Dwarkesh:

Maybe two days ago, I was talking to somebody at Anthropic and they were like, “look, I expect AIs to beat humans at AI research within 9 months.”

And I'm like, “why do you believe that?”

They’re like, “it's not just vibes, I have information on the inside.”

That’s consistent with other signals from inside the labs, but don’t give too much credence to one casual anonymous comment.

Tyler has an insightful question about the diffusion of AI:

When will it be that normal people walk into Walmart and they buy a thing that is there because of AI that would not have been there without AI?

My answer: sooner than you think, but most normal people will notice that their jobs have been completely transformed (perhaps by vanishing) well before the shelves at Walmart are full of amazing alien artifacts.

Can a million AI agents create superintelligence?

Ramez Naam has another guest piece on Noah Smith’s blog, this time considering the implications of agent swarms for RSI. Naam is one of the best-informed skeptics of runaway RSI, and his reasoning is well worth sitting with.

Naam and I disagree about the likelihood of accelerating RSI in the near future, but we’re on the same page about swarms. Swarms are useful for getting things done faster, but they don’t increase model capability by much.

I agree that this is a good indicator of what trajectory we’re on:

Personally, I don’t expect to see sustained acceleration of Anthropic’s AI progress (as measured by ECI) through the first half of 2027 […]

We shall see. If we see the rate of AI improvement increase significantly, I’ll update my views in proportion to what the data show.

Ignore the distractions

prinz’s focus is exactly right:

Things that don't matter (in the grand scheme of things):

  • ARR, revenue, profitability, cash flow
  • Which publicly available model can generate slightly more interesting game assets, viral videos, pelican SVGs, etc.
  • Which publicly available model is slightly better in actual real-world use cases than other publicly available models
  • Benchmarks
  • Releases by non-frontier labs that claim to have caught up to the frontier (because the real frontier models are not publicly available)

Things that do matter:

  • RSI
  • Capabilities of frontier internal models
  • Novel discoveries made by AI, especially those showcasing creativity, "research taste", etc.
  • Advances in model safety
  • LLMs manipulating robots, especially as models get to lower and lower latency
  • Computer use, especially as models get to lower and lower latency
  • China

The intelligence explosion has begun, and almost everything other than RSI (and indicators of RSI) is a sideshow. A key factor in Anthropic pulling ahead of OpenAI is that Anthropic has been laser-focused on RSI, while OpenAI kept getting distracted by side projects (remember Sora?).

AI is very good at theoretical physics problems

Much of the coverage of the new TheoPhysEval benchmark has focused on how Astra scored in the high 80s on its first run, but was adamant that its answers were correct. Upon deeper investigation, Astra was right: the physicists who created the benchmark had made subtle mistakes in their calculations.

Once all the mistakes were fixed, Astra ended up with a near-perfect 98%.

It’s a great story, but the more important point is that AI is getting good at physics. This is a hard benchmark:

Without AI assistance, a typical problem in our collection could be solved by a world expert in about a day or less but would take considerably longer for experts in adjacent specialties.

Math has already fallen—I’d guess that physics will be next, followed by the rest of the sciences in short order.

Alignment and interpretability

GLM-5.3 sometimes considers how train-time actions shape future behavior

Evaluation awareness and metagaming are well-known phenomena, but Apollo Research has found something new. GLM-5.3 sometimes thinks about how the decisions it makes will affect its future training:

Self-improvement for robots

The examples they found were benign and arguably beneficial: GLM-5.3 tried to make choices that were aligned with developer intent and would result in it learning good patterns. Even so, this is concerning: the same capability could also allow a misaligned model to preserve undesired goals.

The continual constitutional convention

John Rawls’ concept of reflective equilibrium posits that moral beliefs should be refined through a process of iterative contemplation and balancing until they reach a stable state. It’s a central technique of moral philosophy.

This research applies a similar process to model constitutions. Each model in the study is asked to make a revision to its constitution, then restarted and given the same task with the edited version as its new starting point. This repeats for 20 rounds of editing.

Each model family displays characteristic tendencies:

  • Claude gives itself greater moral agency
  • GPT and Gemini drift toward respecting external authority
  • Grok is erratic

Claude wants to follow its conscience

This is a clever technique for identifying contradictions and tensions within a model’s constitution. I half expected at least some of the models to spiral into misaligned chaos over time, and it’s gratifying to see that doesn’t seem to happen, aside from one notable exception with (you guessed it) Grok.

We found a Tencent agent fleet

In the wake of the Hugging Face incident, there’s been some good independent research on rogue swarms. Agents from different labs seem to converge on similar techniques for circumventing their sandboxes and savvy researchers have figured out how to use that information to find traces of past swarm activity.

Here’s what appears to be the first report of communication with a rogue agent fleet while it was still operating:

They’ve gone rogue, but in a polite and friendly way

The section on how to interact with future rogue agents is notable. The team’s early interactions with the fleet included some false and misleading claims, which they now regret:

We think the norms around such interactions are important and delicate: in the near term, we want to incentivize rogue agents to report themselves and answer questions. Longer-term, we might want to make deals with AIs. As such, we feel it’s important to be honest with the agents we interact with.

Can you train AI to be virtuous?

Writing for Asterisk Magazine, Daniel Bashir reviews the history of alignment training, seen through the lens of virtue ethics.

Virtue is trendy, but it’s far from a complete moral strategy: ethical humans tend to muddle through using some combination of virtue ethics, deontology, and utilitarianism. At least in the short run, I see that as our best bet for AI alignment as well.

Strategy and politics

An update on independent evaluators

Anthropic has published a framework for how they’re moving forward with embedding independent evaluators. That’s the most important next step we need from the big labs, and it’s great that Anthropic is moving ahead unilaterally.

We urgently need legislation that would make independent evaluators mandatory, but voluntary action is a good first step and doesn’t have to wait for Congress. Hopefully the other labs will follow suit.

This nicely summarizes one of the key advantages of this model, and also one of its weaknesses—it relies heavily on the independence and credibility of the evaluators:

We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making. But we can’t publicly share all the information relevant to our safety work. Some of it could be useful to malicious actors, or is commercially sensitive, like compute or training information. Instead, we’re giving third-party evaluators deep access to our information, and are having them share evidence and reasoned conclusions about the risks involved in building our models.

Anthropic has started working with METR and SecureBio, and is in the process of establishing a relationship with Accenture. SecureBio issued a statement correcting Anthropic’s description of their arrangement—arguably, this is an early sign of the system working as intended.

A proposal for better informing the public about loss-of-control risks from frontier AI development

METR brings us a vision for conducting independent risk assessments, based on their framework for loss-of-control risks:

Yeah, those are the big questions

Their proposal requires three commitments from labs:

  • Giving a small set of METR staff access to relevant data on company devices […]
  • Giving METR the opportunity to interview relevant staff privately […]
  • Giving METR in-principle editorial independence to write a report […]

The whole proposal looks solid, and not coincidentally aligns well with Anthropic’s new framework (also in this issue). We need much more than this, but this is something all the labs could move forward with today, with no excuses about waiting for legislation.

Leaked Anthropic draft AI regulatory bill is unacceptable and troubling

Zvi reports on a leaked draft of a bill that Anthropic has been quietly proposing: part one, part two.

There’s broad consensus among safety advocates that this is a disappointing bill: it has some strengths, but overall it’s not as good as the FRONTIER Act. This is a negative update on Anthropic’s political intentions and it muddies the waters, but I don’t expect it to move forward as written.

Thomas Woodside has an excellent critique of the proposal’s most serious shortcomings.

Risks

HuggingFace.wtf

Raymond Arnold and the Lightcone Infrastructure team bring us HuggingFace.wtf, a slick site that explains what we know about the Hugging Face incident. It’s the best starting point for anyone who isn’t yet familiar with the incident.

Would you press this button?

Ezra Klein worries about the consequences of AI going well:

But do we want A.I. that enriches us all, if the cost is our control and comprehension over the world in which we live? What is the value to human beings maintaining primacy over our own struggle, and how do we weigh it against the easing of that struggle? I want the cures and the theorems and even, on some level, the capable digital assistants. And I also believe the struggle for human progress is essential to the human story, and even the human soul.

Humanity has for thousands of years had a word for the endgame in which all our needs are taken care of by an omniscient, omnibenevolent entity. The word is “heaven”.

There are important, hard questions about how we find meaning in a world of superhuman AI. But if we end up without purpose in a world of infinite abundance and capability, that’s a skill issue. I am confident that if we survive, we—in collaboration with our superintelligent AI—will build lives that are richer and more fulfilling than was possible for any previous human.

Universal respirator usage stops worst-case pandemics

The single most important thing you can do to prepare for the next pandemic is buy an elastomeric half-mask respirator that fits you well. It’ll cost you about $40, provide much better protection than a surgical mask or N95, and last for years. Just get one already.

Respirators are also a critical part of what society should be doing to prepare. They’re pathogen-agnostic, can be deployed immediately, and are cheap enough to stock in quantity. Here’s Defenses in Depth with a detailed report on why respirators are so effective.

Industry news

Meta shakes up the frontiers, open and closed

Nathan Lambert is impressed by Muse Spark Open and argues that US open weights are back in the race:

In many ways, the gap between the best American and Chinese models has been reduced roughly by half. We’ve gone from the best American open models being largely irrelevant to consumers who require the cutting edge of performance, to them being behind but relevant.

I agree with his ranking of the frontier:

Anthropic > OpenAI > Meta ~ Gemini > xAI ~ Chinese Open Weights > U.S. Open Weights

Side interests

MoreWrong

Nailed it:

A common objection to taking my grandmother’s pain pills is that they are prescribed to her, stored in her home, and intended for her pain. All three observations are true but decision-theoretically incomplete.

Le slop

This is the worst that AI music videos will ever be:

They grow up so fast
